title: Causation in Arabic and Islamic Thought

summaries.example: Imagine a piece of cotton near a fire. One thinker might say the fire makes the cotton burn. Another might say God creates the burning whenever the fire and cotton are together. A third might say the fire usually burns cotton, unless something blocks it. These different answers show why philosophers ask what a cause really is.
summaries.summary: From about the ninth to twelfth centuries, theologians and philosophers in Arabic and Islamic thought developed different ideas about causation. They asked whether God alone causes every change, whether people cause their own choices and actions, and whether natural things such as fire have real powers. Muʿtazilites connected human power with divine justice. Ashʿarites stressed divine omnipotence and described human action through acquisition. Philosophers, drawing on Aristotle, studied several kinds of causes and treated causal knowledge as important for science. Avicenna gave a major account in which causes explain and give existence, while al-Ghazālī and Averroes disagreed about necessary connections in nature. The debates also examined choice, miracles, and how observation can teach us about causal powers.
key_ideas: Classical thinkers in Arabic and Islamic traditions debated how events happen and who has the power to make them happen.
Muʿtazilite theologians gave human beings power over their own actions so reward and punishment could be fair.
Ashʿarite theologians emphasized God’s complete power and described human action as something God creates through a person’s temporary power.
Philosophers used Aristotle’s kinds of causes and tried to explain both natural events and God’s relation to the world.
Al-Ghazālī questioned whether fire truly causes burning, while Averroes defended natural causes, especially when nothing blocks them.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates help us understand questions that still matter: How do we explain events? How can people be responsible? Does science discover real powers in nature, or only regular patterns? The thinkers did not all agree, but their careful arguments show why ideas about God, freedom, nature, and knowledge are connected.

important_terms.definition: A cause is something that helps bring about an event or explains why it happens.
Agency is the ability to do something or bring about a change.
A view that says God is the only true cause of events in the created world.
A reason or explanation that is enough to make something happen or to explain why it exists.

questions_to_think_about: When you see one event follow another, what makes you think the first caused the second?
Can a person be responsible for an action if God controls everything?
Could cotton touch fire without burning? Why might someone answer yes or no?

summaries.example: Consider dry cotton placed against fire. Avicenna’s account suggests that fire, suitable cotton, contact, and the absence of obstacles can together form a sufficient cause; once all conditions are present, burning follows necessarily. Al-Ghazālī argues that observation shows only that burning regularly accompanies contact, not that fire has an independent power to produce it. Averroes replies that fire remains a natural cause: contact alone may fail if an impediment, such as a covering, prevents the fire’s action.
summaries.summary: Classical Arabic and Islamic discussions of causation developed through two partly distinct traditions: kalām, or speculative theology, and falsafa, the philosophical tradition shaped by Aristotle and other Greek thinkers. The central theological dispute concerned agency and divine power. Muʿtazilites held that human beings produce at least some actions, since responsibility requires genuine human agency. Ashʿarites rejected this limitation on divine power and explained action through kasb, or acquisition, while broadly tending toward occasionalism. Philosophers instead sought a unified account of natural and divine causation. Avicenna’s influential theory defines the efficient cause as a giver of existence and links causation to the Principle of Sufficient Reason. A complete cause necessitates its effect, although causal priority is not necessarily temporal priority. Avicenna’s view raises questions about freedom and responsibility. Al-Ghazālī challenged the necessity of natural connections, arguing that observation of fire and burning does not prove that fire alone produces burning. Averroes defended natural causation, while acknowledging that conditions and impediments matter. The debates also concern final causation, miracles, divine knowledge, voluntary action, and whether experience can establish causal powers rather than mere regular correlation.
key_ideas: Kalām debates focused on the distribution of agency. Muʿtazilites made human beings genuine sources of certain actions because divine reward and punishment would otherwise seem unjust; Ashʿarites emphasized God’s unrestricted power and developed kasb.

Arabic philosophers adopted Aristotle’s four causes but especially developed accounts of efficient and final causation. Avicenna defined the efficient cause metaphysically as a giver of existence and organized agents hierarchically.

Avicenna connected causation with the Principle of Sufficient Reason: when all conditions needed for an effect are present, the cause necessitates the effect, and cause and effect coexist rather than being related merely by temporal succession.

Al-Ghazālī denied that natural regularities prove necessary connections and used this position to protect divine omnipotence and the possibility of miracles. Averroes defended natural powers while allowing that impediments can prevent an effect.
Later debates asked whether the Principle of Sufficient Reason applies to free choice, whether motives determine action, and whether praise, blame, and responsibility remain useful.

The tradition also examined knowledge of causal powers. Avicenna distinguished simple induction from experience informed by an implicit argument, while al-Ghazālī and Averroes disagreed about what observation establishes.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry shows that theories of causation are not isolated from broader philosophical commitments. Views about what causes an event affect accounts of divine justice, omnipotence, freedom, miracles, scientific knowledge, and moral responsibility. The arguments also anticipate familiar modern problems: whether correlation proves causation, whether deterministic explanations leave room for freedom, and what kind of explanation science seeks.

important_terms.definition: The study of what makes events happen, including different types of explanatory dependence.
In Aristotle’s framework, material, formal, efficient, and final explanations of change or existence.
The efficient cause understood broadly as that which gives existence to something else; Avicenna applies this to natural and creative agents.
The view that every thing has an adequate cause or explanation for its existence or nonexistence.
The doctrine, associated broadly with Ashʿarite theology, that God alone has causal efficacy in the created world.
A theory of human action in which God creates the powers through which a person performs an action, while the person acquires it.
A theory holding that freedom can exist even when actions arise necessarily from an agent’s desires, choices, and conditions.
The idea that repeated observation may not by itself establish a necessary causal connection.

questions_to_think_about: Does regular succession show that one event causes another, or could it show only a dependable pattern?
If a cause necessitates its effect, in what sense can a voluntary action be free?
Can divine omnipotence coexist with stable natural powers?
Why might an efficient cause be defined differently in physics and metaphysics?
Does repeated observation provide certainty, probability, or only evidence requiring further explanation?

summaries.example: Suppose a student chooses between two identical-looking snacks. One view says the choice must have a reason that makes one snack preferable. Another says the will can choose one even when the options seem equal. A Muʿtazilite might stress that the student is truly responsible for the choice. An Ashʿarite might say God creates the power and action, while the student acquires the action. The example helps show why choice, cause, and responsibility were discussed together.
summaries.summary: Between roughly the ninth and twelfth centuries, thinkers in Arabic and Islamic intellectual traditions developed competing accounts of causation. Theologians in kalām focused on God’s justice, power, and relation to human action. Muʿtazilites said human beings produce their own actions, since responsibility requires meaningful agency. Ashʿarī thinkers rejected the idea that this reduces God’s power. They held that God creates the powers through which people act, a position associated with acquisition and often with occasionalism. Philosophers in the falsafa tradition drew on Aristotle’s four causes and treated knowledge of causes as central to science. Avicenna offered a broad theory of efficient causation and argued that causes explain why an effect exists. He also used the Principle of Sufficient Reason, according to which things require adequate explanations. Al-Ghazālī challenged the philosophers’ account of necessary natural connections, especially the claim that fire must burn cotton. Averroes defended natural powers, while noting that an effect may fail when an obstacle is present. Later discussions connected these issues to freedom, miracles, divine knowledge, and the reliability of experience.
key_ideas: Muʿtazilite theologians argued that people cause their own choices and actions, because punishment or reward would be unfair if people had no real agency.
Ashʿarī theologians emphasized divine omnipotence and held that God creates the powers involved in human actions. Their account is often connected with occasionalism.
Philosophers in the falsafa tradition used Aristotle’s four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final. They considered causes important to scientific understanding.
Avicenna developed a powerful account of efficient causes as givers of existence and connected it with the Principle of Sufficient Reason.
Al-Ghazālī argued that seeing fire followed by burning does not prove that fire itself must cause burning. Averroes defended natural causes, while allowing that obstacles can interrupt their effects.
Thinkers disagreed about whether human choices need a determining reason and whether freedom can exist when actions have causes.
summaries.why_it_matters: These arguments help explain why people can disagree about the same event while using careful reasoning. They also connect everyday questions—such as whether a choice was really ours—to larger questions about nature, God, science, and responsibility. Studying the debate teaches us to separate what we observe from what we conclude about causes.

important_terms.definition: Something that brings about an event or gives an explanation for why it occurs.
The power to perform an action or produce a change.
The belief that God is the only genuine cause of events, even when events appear to be caused by natural things.
The view that a person’s action is connected with God’s creation of a temporary power through which the person acts.
A principle saying that everything has an adequate reason or cause for existing or not existing.
An explanation based on the goal or purpose for which something happens.

questions_to_think_about: If people do not cause their own actions, can praise and blame still make sense?
Does fire really cause burning, or do we only observe that burning usually follows contact with fire?
What is the difference between a cause and a purpose?
Can an action be free if it has a sufficient cause?
Why might a philosopher want one theory that explains both natural and divine causation?
